newsitem.title: GERMANY: German air cargo rates to Asia up, market recovers.
newsitem.headline: German air cargo rates to Asia up, market recovers.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Germany to destinations in Asia have risen sharply at the start of March, a Reuters' survey showed.
Official rates have been increased between five and 10 percent by most carriers to key Asian gateway destinations such as Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore and Bangkok, industry sources said.
Soaring demand for Japan, a slump in exports to Korea and the promise of strong growth for India are the key market trends at present, they reported.
The rise in the value of the dollar against the German mark has also reduced import prices for clients and thus boosted air cargo exports from Germany.
The market pick-up has been prompted by good business in February after a mixed January, forwarders, airline managers and sales agents told Reuters.
Wolfgang Kulenkampff, Thyssen Haniel Logistic (THL) board member for air cargo, said: "At present the export trade is booming and imports are weaker.

He added: "The market outlook is not so rosy. I see business growing five to eight percent but that depends on whether we can put through the rates increase and we will see that over the coming weeks and months."
Thomas Reuter, Frankfurt manager of Dachser Airfreight, warned it might not be easy to pass on the rates rises to shippers who wanted to plan transport costs long-term.
"Carriers are trying to use the market situation with big jumps in rates but that makes business difficult for us," he said.
Lufthansa Cargo sales manager Germany, Florian Pfaff, said the airline was optimistic about prospects for the coming months.
"I believe the rates rises will be carried by agents. The market is generally going well and that makes talks on rates rises easier," he noted.
Pfaff added: "We are benefitting from the dollar development and the market is better. The dollar trend is good for exports."
Oliver Evans, KLM sales director central and eastern Europe, said KLM raised ex-Germany rates by 5-10 percent from March 1.
"I think the market was expecting increases. Demand for capacity has grown so rates have increased," he said.
Evans added: "We have seen an increase in demand and expect a relatively firm January and February. We expect a small market rise for the first two months of the year."
British Airways has increased its ex-Germany rates to India, Singapore, Japan, Korea and China by up to 10 percent from March 1 but left other Asian destinations unchanged.
Mark Gardiner, cargo manager Central Europe, said: "I think forwarders will accept the higher rates, there is an understanding that rates need to be pushed up."
The market had picked up in recent weeks after a slow start to the year and prospects looked good for the rest of 1997, he added.
A short-term boost to German air cargo exports to Japan has been given by the rise in Japanese consumption tax to five percent from three percent due from April 1, sources said.
Dachser's Reuter said demand for Japan had clearly picked up, which could be a reaction by importers seeking to beat to the forthcoming consumption tax change deadline.
"The Far East is pretty full. There is quite a lot of freight on the market at present," he noted.
Lufthansa's Pfaff noted that demand for Japan had risen strongly in early 1997 with double-figure growth rates.
Nippon Cargo Airlines (NCA.CN) said it has increased rates to Japan by seven percent effective March 1.
Meinholf Weiden, sales manager Germany, said the rise was prompted by soaring market demand, tight space and internal demands for a better yield.
"The tax consumption in Japan will rise to five percent from three percent from April so many companies are trying to increase imports in March to avoid this," he told Reuters.
German air cargo exports to South Korea are starting to pick up again after a weak start to 1997, sources said.
Korean Air said it raised ex-Germany rates by 6-12 percent from March 1 with lower rises to Korea and south-east Asia and more to Japan.
Germany cargo sales manager, Robert M. Instinsky, said demand for Korea had picked up after a slow start to 1997 in the wake of the recent disturbances and the collapse of the Hanbo Group.
"January was not so good but February has gone superbly well. We are very full," he said.
Instinsky added: "We think that demand for Japan will rise in March but it is too early to say if the consumption tax change will have an effect."
The Frankfurt manager of a major German forwarder noted that shipments to Korea improved in February after a poor January due to the Chinese New Year.
The market to Hong Kong and China has been subdued following the December 1996 boom prompted by changes in import duties.
Dachser airfreight manager Thomas Reuter said: "Demand is growing for Hong Kong but it is not clear whether that is something to do with the July handover."
Another forwarder noted: "China has tailed off a little at the start of this year because demand is not so high as in December when all contracts had to be completed by December 31."
The launch of a direct Martinair (MART.CN) freighter to Guangzhou was an interesting innovation, he said.
"Martinair is an airline with good offers and by the end of this year a lot of shipments which go through Hong Kong will go directly into China," he forecast.
EVA Air Germany sales manager Pei-Fang Wagner said: "The market to the Far East is going very well at the moment."
The Taiwanese carrier would maintain its rates to follow market development before possibly raising them in mid-March, she added.
The sales manager of one large German forwarder described demand for south-east Asia as "difficult" at present.
Malaysian Airline System (MAS) said it will hold back an ex-Germany rates rise of up to 20 percent until April.
Peter Skaryd, MAS cargo sales executive Germany, said: "We are going to increase 10-20 percent to Asian destinations, not in March but from April."
Ramadan and Chinese New Year meant cargo volumes to Malaysia had been relatively quiet in February since many shipments had been postponed, he said.
Thai Airways said it raised ex-Germany cargo rates by 5-8 percent from March 1 with a five percent across the board rise for south-east Asia and eight per cent hike to Japan.
Germany cargo sales manager, Guillermo Valencia, said load factors had not been so good in February but the rising dollar could boost German exports in the coming months.
"What is missing is freight to Korea at present. But I do not believe demand is being impacted by the internal political situation," he said.
The market to India could pick up over the coming months following cuts in import duties announced in last week's budget, sources said.
Air India (AIN.CN) warned it could run short of cargo capacity in April due to the suspension of three of its five weekly Germany flights from March 8 in order to fly Moslem pilgrims to Saudi Arabia.

Cargo sales manager Germany, Ruediger Brasche, forecast: "From April (tonnage) could increase substantially if import conditions in India are made more flexible. Cargo could rise 50 percent from a reduction in import duties.".
"The year has begun excellently but we have still struggled with too little capacity. We could have flown much more," he added.
Brasche said rates from Germany had now achieved much better levels following large-scale hikes by Lufthansa, Air India and other carriers at the start of January.
But Dachser's Reuter said: "Rates have increased so dramatically it is difficult to see if they will be accepted by the market. Many importers are switching to cheap carriers in order to pay less."
Saana-based Yemenia has won new cargo clients by under-cutting market rates up to 60 percent for Germany to India freight, Ingo Zimmer, manager of gsa ATC Aviation Services, said.
"With Yemenia we did not increase rates. We kept prices low to win clients since we wanted to show them we could offer a good service with these prices."
But rates would rise about 20 percent from April 1 when an Airbus A310 with space for 10 tonnes replaced a B727 on the twice-weekly Frankfurt-Sanaa flight which connected to Bombay flights, he added.
